extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to word and publish corrections/clarifications for news organizations, including whether to repeat the original error and how to label notices across print and online editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether to restate the original error
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of whether to repeat the error in a correction has long been debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author supports stating the initial error: 'I support stating the initial error, as it ensures people understand clearly what was incorrect.' Restating the original mistake ensures readers know what was wrong and can make the correction meaningful (and, as noted, can lead to 'funnier corrections'). Anti-pattern: leaving readers guessing by omitting the original erroneous wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling: 'correction' versus 'clarification'
rubrics_metrics.description: The online version is labeled a 'clarification,' while the print version uses wording of a correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate label ('correction' or 'clarification') that matches the substance of the notice. Labels affect reader expectations: a 'clarification' that omits the original error can leave readers unclear about what changed. Be consistent in label usage and ensure the label aligns with whether the original error is being restated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in wording: state what was incorrect and what the correct information is
rubrics_metrics.description: Print correction clearly states the initial, mistaken description of Capt. Durand; the online version leaves you guessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write corrections that explicitly identify the incorrect statement and provide the corrected version (example: 'An earlier version of this article incorrectly described Navy Capt. Robert Durand’s physical build. He should have been described as muscular. This version has been corrected.'). Avoid vague phrasing that fails to convey the substance of the error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across platforms (print and online)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications typically decide to restate the error (as the New York Times does), or to avoid restating it, and then they stick to that style. The Post is doing one thing in print, and the another online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a single house approach to corrections and apply it consistently across print and digital editions, or clearly explain departures. Inconsistency between platforms can confuse readers and undermine credibility; if different approaches are used, document the rationale and communicate it to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a statement that the piece has been corrected/updated
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an explicit line indicating the article version has been corrected (e.g., 'This version has been corrected.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End correction notices with an explicit statement that the version has been corrected or updated so readers know the change has been implemented. This helps track that remedial action occurred and signals accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability in corrections practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating the initial error ensures people understand clearly what was incorrect and supports press freedom and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor transparency (identifying the original error and the correction) as a principle because it clarifies facts for readers and demonstrates institutional accountability. Transparency is also offered as a normative justification for preferring restatement of errors over omission.
